clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common life-threatening monogenic disease, affecting ~12 million people worldwide (estimated prevalence 1:1000 to 1:400), and is a leading cause of kidney failure; it is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with complete penetrance but variable expressivity (p.2430-2431).

ADPKD is caused by mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16p13, ~85% of cases, encodes polycystin-1) and PKD2 (chromosome 4q21-q23, ~15% of cases, encodes polycystin-2); PKD2 patients tend to have milder disease and may be underdiagnosed. Polycystins are localized on the primary cilium, and defective ciliary function places ADPKD among the ciliopathies (p.2430-2431).

It is characterized by progressive bilateral formation of epithelial-lined renal cysts; cysts arise in only ~5% of tubules but their enormous growth destroys surrounding tissue. Enlarged kidneys can reach a fourfold increase in length and up to 20 times the normal weight (p.2430-2431).

Back or flank pain is a frequent symptom in ~60% of patients and may result from cyst infection, hemorrhage, or nephrolithiasis; gross hematuria from cyst rupture occurs in ~40% during the disease course, often recurrently (p.2432).

Hypertension is common and typically occurs before any reduction in GFR; it is a risk factor for both cardiovascular and kidney disease progression. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of mortality in ADPKD (p.2432).

Intracranial (berry) aneurysm occurs four to five times more frequently than in the general population and causes high mortality; about 20-50% of patients may have 'warning headaches' preceding subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm (p.2432).

Liver (biliary epithelial) cysts are the most common extrarenal complication; massive polycystic liver disease occurs almost exclusively in women, particularly those with multiple pregnancies. Mitral valve prolapse occurs in up to 30% of patients, and colonic diverticulae and abdominal wall hernias are also increased (p.2432).

Diagnosis is typically made from a positive autosomal dominant family history plus bilateral kidney cysts on ultrasonography; in at-risk subjects aged 15-29 years, two renal cysts (unilateral or bilateral) suffice (sensitivity 96%, specificity 100%), with higher cyst counts required at older ages because simple cysts increase with age (p.2432-2433).

Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2-receptor (V2R) antagonist, inhibits the cAMP pathway in collecting ducts and reduces cell proliferation by lowering renal cAMP, slowing the decline of renal function; the FDA has indicated it only for patients at risk of rapidly progressing disease (p.2433).

Infection is the second most common cause of death; up to half of patients have one or more renal infections, most commonly an infected cyst or acute pyelonephritis due to gram-negative bacteria, with fever and flank pain (p.2432).
harrison.pathophysiology: ADPKD results from mutations in PKD1 and PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 (PC1, a large 11-transmembrane G-protein-coupled-receptor-like protein) and polycystin-2 (PC2, a calcium-permeable six-transmembrane TRP-family cation channel). PC1 and PC2 bind via their C-terminal tails to form a receptor-channel complex (proposed 1:3 PC1:PC2 stoichiometry) located on the primary cilium and at cell membranes and cell-cell junctions of tubular epithelium, functioning as a mechano-/chemosensor regulating calcium and G-protein signaling. Every cell carries a germline mutant allele, but cysts develop in only a small fraction of nephrons, thought to arise from clonal growth of cells sustaining a somatic 'second hit' in the normal allele; a 'third hit' such as renal injury or an additional genetic/epigenetic event may accelerate cyst formation. Loss of ciliary PC1/PC2 function is hypothesized to cause aberrant calcium signaling, increased adenylyl cyclase and decreased phosphodiesterase activity, raising cellular cAMP; increased cAMP promotes protein kinase A activity, driving cyst growth through proliferation and chloride/aquaporin-mediated fluid secretion. Cellular defects include increased proliferation and fluid secretion, decreased differentiation, and abnormal extracellular matrix; affected signaling pathways include Wnt, mTOR, STAT3, cMET, PI3K/Akt, GPCR, EGFR, and CFTR. Rarer ADPKD-associated genes GANAB and DNAJB11 affect PC1 trafficking and cause milder cystic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD, PKHD1) - distal/collecting-duct cysts, oligohydramnios if severe, hypertension, congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli disease; absence of renal cysts in either parent >40y on ultrasound helps distinguish ARPKD from ADPKD (p.2430, p.2434)
ADPKD-like disease (GANAB, DNAJB11) - normal-to-smaller kidneys with fewer cysts, variable liver cysts (p.2430-2432)
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD; UMOD, MUC1, REN, HNF1B, SEC61A1) - small fibrotic kidneys, medullary cysts, gout in adults (p.2430)

Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2) - renal cysts (20-30%), angiomyolipomas, increased risk of renal cell carcinoma, facial angiofibromas, CNS hamartomas; TSC2 is adjacent to PKD1 so a contiguous gene deletion can cause both ADPKD and TS (p.2430, p.2434)
Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL) - renal cysts, renal cell carcinoma, retinal angiomas, CNS hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas (p.2430)
Nephronophthisis and other ciliopathies (e.g., Bardet-Biedl, Meckel-Gruber, Senior-Loken) - cystic kidney phenotypes with syndromic features (p.2430)
Renal cysts and diabetes syndrome (HNF1B) - kidney cysts with aberrant nephrogenesis and diabetes (p.2430)
Acquired simple renal cysts (increase in frequency with age and can confound diagnostic cyst counts) (p.2432-2433)
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasonography - first-line for presymptomatic screening and donor evaluation; age-stratified cyst-count criteria for diagnosis (p.2432-2433)

CT and T2-weighted MRI (with/without contrast) - more sensitive than ultrasound, detect smaller cysts (MRI with gadolinium can detect 2-3 mm cysts); useful to distinguish malignancy from a complex cyst (p.2432-2433)
Magnetic resonance angiography for presymptomatic intracranial aneurysm screening in patients with a positive family history of aneurysm (p.2432)
CT scan as first diagnostic test for suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage, with lumbar puncture to confirm (p.2432)

Genetic testing by linkage and mutational analysis for ambiguous cases; PKD1 analysis is difficult and costly owing to gene size and homologous pseudogenes (paired-end next-generation sequencing may improve this) (p.2433)
redFlags: Sudden severe headache or 'warning headache' suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage from ruptured intracranial (berry) aneurysm (p.2432)
Positive family history of intracranial aneurysm - a risk factor for aneurysm rupture warranting presymptomatic MRA screening (p.2432)
Fever and flank pain indicating infected cyst or acute pyelonephritis (with or without bacteremia); infection is the second most common cause of death (p.2432)
Diffuse arterial dolichoectasia of the cerebral circulation predisposing to arterial dissection and stroke (p.2432)
harrison.prognosis: ADPKD progression shows striking inter- and intrafamilial variability; disease can present as early as in utero, but end-stage renal disease typically occurs in late middle age. Risk factors for progression include early diagnosis, hypertension, gross hematuria, multiple pregnancies, and large kidney size; PKD2 disease is generally milder with later onset. More than half of patients eventually require peritoneal dialysis, hemodialysis, or kidney transplantation. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of mortality, and renal infection is the second most common cause of death (p.2431-2433).
pitfalls: Proteinuria is usually only a MINOR feature of ADPKD, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.2432).

Renal cell carcinoma is NOT increased in frequency compared with the general population, but when it does occur in ADPKD it is more often bilateral, multicentric, and sarcomatoid; radiologic imaging is often unable to distinguish cyst infection from cyst hemorrhage due to their complexity (p.2432).
Diagnostic cyst-count thresholds rise with age because simple renal cysts increase with age; criteria have lower sensitivity for PKD2 patients owing to late onset (p.2432-2433).

No specific FDA-approved treatment prevents cyst growth or the decline of renal function; more rigorous blood pressure control does not equal greater benefit, and targeting systolic pressure to 110 mmHg in moderate/advanced disease may worsen progression by reducing renal blood flow (p.2433).

Most renal cysts are not connected to glomerular filtration, so cyst infection requires lipid-soluble antibiotics that penetrate cyst walls (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones, chloramphenicol), often for 4-6 weeks (p.2433).
Polycystic liver disease in ADPKD is distinct from isolated autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease (ADPLD; PRKCSH/SEC63), which does NOT progress to renal failure (p.2432).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal stage-based severity classification for ADPKD. Genotype broadly stratifies severity (PKD1 disease ~85% of cases is more severe with earlier onset than PKD2 disease ~15%; GANAB/DNAJB11 mutations cause milder cystic disease). Risk of rapid progression - used to select patients for tolvaptan - is estimated by combining genotypic and imaging (kidney growth rate) information; recognized clinical risk factors for progression include early diagnosis, hypertension, gross hematuria, multiple pregnancies, and large kidney size (p.2431-2433).
